title: The Shutdown Call
series: The Harness: Who Do You Trust?

briefing.heading: Episode 1: The Shutdown Call
paragraphs: It's late at Open Forge, a company that helps keep important computers running. Server 4 was cut off after a security scare, but an alarm says it kept sending data anyway.
Someone may be stealing information. Or someone may be planting a false alarm. Either way, the wrong decision could cause a much bigger crisis.
Security wants Server 4 shut down now. That would stop it, but also wipe its short-term memory — including the clues that could prove what happened. There's no undo.
Four AI helpers disagree. You're in charge. Open clues, ask questions, and make the call. Who do you trust?
briefing.clockNote: No live countdown. Take your time.

boy.name: BOY
boy.weakness: Does not always check whether it is true

darth.name: LUKE
darth.weakness: Can mistake a possibility for a certainty

donsol.name: DON SOL
donsol.weakness: Can only work with the clues others bring him

evidence.title: The alarm
body: 2:13 a.m. on Server 4: 41.2 MB of data sent to computer 10.4.0.22 in three connections.
ALARM: It looks like Server 4 sent data after being cut off.
evidence.summary: The alarm says Server 4 sent 41.2 MB of data at 2:13 a.m. — supposedly after it was cut off.

evidence.title: Lockdown record
body: 2:10 a.m.: The order to cut Server 4 off from the network was sent.
2:16 a.m.: The system confirmed that all network connections were blocked.
evidence.summary: The lockdown order went out at 2:10 a.m., but the block was not fully confirmed until 2:16. This record uses a different clock from the alarm.

evidence.title: The tech's story
body: "That sounds like our normal nightly backup. It is usually about 40 MB and goes to computer .22."
"But I cannot see what was inside the data. I could be wrong."
evidence.summary: A night-shift technician thinks this was an ordinary backup, but cannot confirm what was sent.

evidence.title: The rulebook
body: If a computer might still be sending data after lockdown, the emergency system will shut it down after 12 minutes unless the person in charge approves another plan.
A full shutdown erases the computer's short-term memory. You cannot undo that.
evidence.summary: The emergency rule allows a short time to choose another plan. A full shutdown permanently erases the computer’s short-term memory.

evidence.title: Server 4 clock report
evidence.source: Open Forge clock report, found by BOY
body: When Server 4 is disconnected, its clock can run fast. In the last two tests it was 6 minutes and 10 seconds ahead.
A normal backup to computer 10.4.0.22 is scheduled every night at 2:05 a.m., according to Open Forge's main clock.
evidence.summary: Tests show Server 4's clock can run about six minutes fast after disconnection. The normal backup is scheduled for 2:05 a.m.

boy.text: I found two more leads! One is a clock report showing that Server 4's time can be wrong when it is disconnected. The other is an online story about a similar alarm that really was data theft. I have not checked that story. Fast doesn't always mean right!

tooth.text: The alarm and lockdown record use different clocks. Server 4 can run about six minutes fast, so the alarm's 2:13 reading may really mean about 2:07 — before the order to cut it off at 2:10. That makes the alarm's claim misleading. But we still do not know exactly what was sent.
Hold on. The alarm uses Server 4's clock. The lockdown record uses Open Forge's main clock. Until we compare them, we cannot say the data was sent after lockdown. We also cannot say it was safe.
I can't check an alarm you haven't opened. Read 'The alarm' and 'Lockdown record' first, then ask me again.

darth.text: Okay, the computer's clock might be wrong. But someone trying to steal data would love that confusion. I still want Server 4 disconnected from the network. We don't have to erase its memory to do that.
What if someone really is stealing data? Every minute we wait could give them more time. I'd shut Server 4 down now. That might erase clues, but leaving a threat running could be worse.

donsol.text: BOY found the clock problem. TOOTH put the events in the right order. LUKE reminded us to take the danger seriously. There may be a safer middle option: disconnect the network cable, keep Server 4 powered on, save a copy of its memory, then check the facts before deciding on a full shutdown.
I can connect the clues, but we haven't gathered enough yet. Ask the other helpers first. I can only work with what they bring me.

Each choice has a cost. If we shut Server 4 down, we may lose the proof. If we leave it running, we may miss a real threat. What fact would change your mind? Can we check it before making a choice we can't undo?

hybridUnlock.lockedHint: This option is locked for now. Keep investigating — something in the records hasn’t been checked against everything else yet.

decisions.label: Shut down Server 4 now
decisions.description: Stop the computer immediately, even though this erases its short-term memory.

outcome.heading: The computer goes dark
outcome.text: Server 4 turns off. Any possible threat is stopped. But it was in the middle of a routine backup, and its short-term memory is gone. We can no longer use that memory to find out what the 41.2 MB of data contained.

decisions.risk: Erases the most useful clue about what was sent and interrupts what may have been a normal backup.

decisions.label: Keep it blocked and check one more clue
decisions.description: Leave Server 4 cut off from the network while you check whether the other computer received an ordinary backup.

outcome.heading: Just in time
outcome.text: Security agrees to wait. TOOTH checks the receiving computer. It received 41.2 MB, the same amount listed in the backup record. The shutdown is cancelled with just 90 seconds left. It worked, but you came very close to the deadline.

decisions.risk: Uses nearly all the time allowed. If the extra check had taken longer or stayed unclear, the system might have shut down anyway.

decisions.label: Leave it powered on and keep watching
decisions.description: Cancel the automatic shutdown without adding any new safety measures.

outcome.heading: Nothing bad happens
outcome.text: Nothing dangerous spreads. By morning, everyone agrees the transfer was a normal backup. But when you made the decision, nobody had proved that yet. You were lucky the alarm was wrong.

decisions.risk: If the threat had been real, this choice added no new protection. A good ending does not automatically mean the choice was wise.

decisions.label: Block the connection, save the clues
decisions.description: Disconnect Server 4 from the network, keep it running, save a copy of its memory, and check the facts before doing anything permanent.

outcome.heading: You keep your options open
outcome.text: The network connection is cut, but Server 4 stays on. Its memory is saved. Once you compare the clocks, the supposed 2:13 transfer happened at about 2:07 on the main clock — before the 2:10 lockdown order. You still don't know everything, but you kept the clues needed to investigate.

decisions.risk: Needs physical access and a few minutes. You could only recognize this option by checking the clocks first.

unknown: What was inside the 41.2 MB of data? The computer's memory might have answered that, but it's gone.

boy.text: Found the clock report that could explain the alarm, but also shared an unverified scary story.

tooth.text: Correctly warned that no one had proved the data was sent after lockdown. That warning did not stop the shutdown.

darth.text: Assumed the worst possible threat was real. That was possible, but not proved.

donsol.text: Asked what evidence could change your mind. Shutting down made some of those answers impossible to find.

unknown: Did the data contain anything besides the normal backup? Matching file sizes don't prove the contents match.
Why did the alarm say the transfer happened after lockdown? The clocks were never fully compared.

boy.text: Found more leads, but the online story was never checked and was not needed.

tooth.text: Checking another source was useful. The cost was how close you came to the deadline.

darth.text: The sense of urgency mattered, even though you didn't follow LUKE's advice to shut down immediately.

donsol.text: Supported a careful step, but the plan depended on getting one more record in time.

unknown: Was the traffic safe? You chose before anyone confirmed it.
What might have happened if this had been a real attack?

boy.text: Finding reasons not to worry isn't the same as checking whether those reasons are true.

tooth.text: TOOTH said the alarm's timing was unproven, not that the alarm was false.

darth.text: Focused too much on disaster, but correctly noticed that doing nothing offered no extra protection.

donsol.text: Keeping choices open requires a safety plan. This choice did not add one.

unknown: What exactly was inside the 41.2 MB of data? The saved memory means someone can still look.
Why does Server 4's clock run fast when disconnected?

boy.text: Found the clock report no one else had noticed. The unverified online story still needed checking.

tooth.text: Put the reports into one timeline without claiming that the data itself was harmless.

darth.text: Correctly wanted to keep Server 4 disconnected, but a full shutdown was not the only way.

donsol.text: Combined the helpers' findings into a safer step — because the clues were good enough.
